title: Artistic investments
titleChinese: 投资艺术品就肯定有回报？
paragraphs: We all have a different approach to money – some of us like to spend it as soon as we have it, even splashing the cash on extravagant things, while some of us like to hold on to it and spend it carefully. But for people who are very savvy about their cash, there are a number of interesting ways to invest it and, if things go well, make a tidy profit.

Buying stamps, wine, coins and books are all different ways of investing your money. It comes with risks but can be thrilling as, hopefully, you watch the value of your investment rise. However, you need to know what you're doing and making your fortune is not guaranteed.

If you're happy to take a gamble, then one of the most well-known ways of investing is by buying artwork. By purchasing a painting and holding on to it, its value can increase by a handsome sum, but of course it's only when you sell it do you feel the financial benefit. Some people get quite lucky, particularly when they don't expect to make any money. There are stories of people buying a painting in an antique shop for peanuts only to find out it's actually worth thousands of pounds.

Investing in art appears to be a hobby for the rich, but not always. Recently, an investor's dream came true when a picture believed to have been painted by Leonardo da Vinci sold for £341m. He had bought it about 60 years ago in an auction for just £45 thinking it was only painted by a follower of da Vinci.

Of course this is a rare story and investing in artwork is not a guarantee to make you a millionaire. Patrick Connolly, a financial adviser at Chase de Vere, told BBC News that to invest in art as a true investment, "you need a starting fund of at least £5,000, and possibly up to £500,000, which can be used to buy individual works of art or invested in an art fund." He feels investing in art is too risky and recommends their clients not to invest in it because the downsides outweigh the upsides.

But if you're still keen, there are art fairs, such as The Affordable Art Fair, and websites aimed at buyers with a modest budget. Patrick Connolly says the best approach here is to buy something you like and can afford and "if it goes up in value, that should be just an added bonus." If this has spoilt your plans for your investment portfolio, maybe there's more chance of winning big money by buying a lottery ticket!

title: The dogs who safeguard our hearts
titleChinese: 养狗能保护我们的心脏健康
paragraphs: As a dog lover, our canine companions always fill me with joy. Whether pedigree or mongrel, tame or stray, whenever I see one, I smile. After all, their loyalty is indisputable, their companionship is always welcome, they fetch for us, guard for us and even work for us when required. Good old Fido has always been close to my, and many other’s hearts.

Well, not content with just warming the cockles of your heart, it seems that our four-legged-friends actually lower the risk of cardiovascular disease, according to a 2017 scientific study, which looked at 3.4 million Swedes from 2001 to 2012.

The study concluded that this lower risk, which was particularly evident in owners of hunting breeds, may not just be due to the increased physical activity that goes hand-in-hand with owning a dog, but could also be down to dogs increasing the owner’s social contact, or by changing the owner's bacterial microbiome, which is the collection of microscopic species that live in the gut. Dogs change the dirt in home environments and therefore expose people to bacteria that they would otherwise not encounter.

These effects were particularly marked in those who lived on their lonesome. According to Mwenya Mubanga of Uppsala University and lead author of the study, “single dog owners had a 33% reduction in risk of death and an 11% reduction in risk of cardiac arrest compared to single non-owners.”

However, before your heart skips a beat, Tove Fall, senior author of the study, also adds that there may be limitations. It’s possible that the differences between owners and non-owners, which already existed before the dog was bought, could have influenced the results – or that people who are generally more active also tend to get a dog anyway.

It seems that the results are not as clear cut as they initially appear to be, but as far as I’m concerned, that’s ok. I love dogs for how they make me feel and, cardiovascular benefits or not, they’ll always be top dog to me – cross my heart.

sentences.english: As a dog lover, our canine companions always fill me with joy.
sentences.chinese: 作为一个爱狗人士，我们的犬类（canine）伙伴总是让我满心欢喜。

sentences.english: Whether pedigree or mongrel, tame or stray, whenever I see one, I smile.
sentences.chinese: 无论是纯种狗（pedigree）还是混血狗（mongrel），温顺的还是流浪的，每当我看到一只狗，我都会微笑。

sentences.english: After all, their loyalty is indisputable, their companionship is always welcome, they fetch for us, guard for us and even work for us when required.
sentences.chinese: 毕竟，它们的忠诚是无可争议的（indisputable），它们的陪伴总是令人欣然接受的，它们为我们叼东西，为我们看家，甚至在需要的时候为我们工作。

sentences.english: Good old Fido has always been close to my, and many other’s hearts.
sentences.chinese: 可爱的老狗狗一直深受我和许多人的喜爱。

sentences.english: Well, not content with just warming the cockles of your heart, it seems that our four-legged-friends actually lower the risk of cardiovascular disease, according to a 2017 scientific study, which looked at 3.4 million Swedes from 2001 to 2012.
sentences.chinese: 嗯，我们的这些四条腿的朋友们可不满足于仅仅温暖你的内心深处，根据2017年的一项科学研究，它们实际上还能降低心血管（cardiovascular）疾病的风险。这项研究对2001年至2012年间的340万瑞典人进行了调查。

sentences.english: The study concluded that this lower risk, which was particularly evident in owners of hunting breeds, may not just be due to the increased physical activity that goes hand-in-hand with owning a dog, but could also be down to dogs increasing the owner’s social contact, or by changing the owner's bacterial microbiome, which is the collection of microscopic species that live in the gut.
sentences.chinese: 研究得出结论，这种风险的降低在猎犬的主人身上尤为明显，这可能不仅仅是因为和狗同行会增加身体活动量，还可能归因于（down to）狗狗增加了主人的社交接触，或者改变了主人的细菌微生物群（bacterial microbiome），也就是生活在肠道内的微观物种的集合。

sentences.english: Dogs change the dirt in home environments and therefore expose people to bacteria that they would otherwise not encounter.
sentences.chinese: 狗狗会改变家庭环境中的尘埃，因此会让人们接触到原本不会遇到的细菌。

sentences.english: These effects were particularly marked in those who lived on their lonesome.
sentences.chinese: 这些影响在那些独自（lonesome）生活的人身上尤为显著。

sentences.english: According to Mwenya Mubanga of Uppsala University and lead author of the study, “single dog owners had a 33% reduction in risk of death and an 11% reduction in risk of cardiac arrest compared to single non-owners.”
sentences.chinese: 根据乌普萨拉大学（Uppsala University）的姆温亚・穆班加（Mwenya Mubanga），也就是这项研究的第一作者所说：“与没有养狗的单身人士相比，养狗的单身人士死亡风险降低了33%，心脏骤停的风险降低了11%。”

sentences.english: However, before your heart skips a beat, Tove Fall, senior author of the study, also adds that there may be limitations.
sentences.chinese: 然而，在你感到开心兴奋之前，这项研究的资深作者托芙・法尔（Tove Fall）也补充说，可能存在一些局限性。

sentences.english: It’s possible that the differences between owners and non-owners, which already existed before the dog was bought, could have influenced the results – or that people who are generally more active also tend to get a dog anyway.
sentences.chinese: 有可能在购买狗之前，养狗者和不养狗者之间已经存在的差异就有可能已经影响了研究结果——或者那些通常更活跃的人无论如何也更倾向于养狗。

sentences.english: It seems that the results are not as clear cut as they initially appear to be, but as far as I’m concerned, that’s ok.
sentences.chinese: 似乎研究结果并不像最初看起来那样明确（clear cut），但就我而言，这没关系。

sentences.english: I love dogs for how they make me feel and, cardiovascular benefits or not, they’ll always be top dog to me – cross my heart.
sentences.chinese: 我爱狗是因为它们给我的感觉，而且不管有没有心血管方面的益处，它们在我心中永远都是最重要的（top dog）——我发誓。

title: Can men dance
titleChinese: 男性会跳舞吗？
paragraphs: Are men able to dance? Well, if I am an example, then no – I have two left feet and taking to the dance floor just fills me with dread. But of course, we know that most of us have the potential to throw some shapes, so what is it that's stopping us?

If you've ever watched glamorous and glitzy dance shows on TV, like the BBC's Strictly Come Dancing, you'll know that there are men who have great dexterity and fancy footwork on the dancefloor. These professional dancers have spent years learning and performing ballroom dances such as the waltz, foxtrot and tango.

But for a majority of us men, we still prefer to spectate rather than participate. And according to a survey commissioned by BBC Radio 5 live, over three quarters of British men have never or rarely danced. It found that over a third of men surveyed wouldn't strut their stuff, let alone perform a paso doble, on the dancefloor because they were too embarrassed. And ten per cent said what put them off was fear of being the centre of attention, being made fun of, or being judged.

Women may say we have to get a grip, get on our feet and just let ourselves go! Easier said than done. But what helps is a crowded dancefloor where there is safety in numbers. And according to the survey, many men need a drink. One man questioned said, "I don't think I'm very good at it and therefore need some Dutch courage to get me on the floor."

One place where the alcohol is flowing is usually at a wedding, so, maybe unsurprisingly, the BBC survey found that 75% of men had previously danced at one. These are also the situations where partners of boyfriends and husbands can persuade them to move to the groove of the music! However, this is the time to witness some 'dad dancing' which is defined in the Oxford English Dictionary as: "An awkward, unfashionable, or unrestrained style of dancing to pop music, as characteristically performed by middle-aged or older men." Surely that's not me!

So let's face it, us men just need help. We need training, we need to practise and we need to lose our inhibitions. One convert, Gareth Dew, who took part in the survey, says, "I think to be able to dance you need to be able to let loose, be aware of your body and generally be more comfortable in yourself." Would you agree?

sentences.english: Are men able to dance?

sentences.english: But of course, we know that most of us have the potential to throw some shapes, so what is it that's stopping us?
sentences.chinese: 但当然，我们知道我们大多数人都有展示舞姿的潜力，那么是什么阻止了我们呢？

sentences.english: If you've ever watched glamorous and glitzy dance shows on TV, like the BBC's Strictly Come Dancing, you'll know that there are men who have great dexterity and fancy footwork on the dancefloor.
sentences.chinese: 如果你曾经在电视上看过迷人又炫目的舞蹈节目，比如BBC的《舞动奇迹》（Strictly Come Dancing），你就会知道，有些男人在舞池里舞步花俏且灵活，和花式的舞步。

sentences.english: These professional dancers have spent years learning and performing ballroom dances such as the waltz, foxtrot and tango.
sentences.chinese: 这些专业舞者花了数年时间学习和表演华尔兹、狐步舞和探戈等交际舞。

sentences.english: But for a majority of us men, we still prefer to spectate rather than participate.
sentences.chinese: 但对于我们大多数男人来说，我们仍然更喜欢观看（spectate）而不是参与。

sentences.english: And according to a survey commissioned by BBC Radio 5 live, over three quarters of British men have never or rarely danced.
sentences.chinese: 根据BBC第五电台（BBC Radio 5 live）委托进行的一项调查，超过四分之三的英国男人从未或很少跳舞。

sentences.chinese: 10%的人表示，让他们排斥的原因是害怕成为关注的焦点、被人取笑或被人评判。

sentences.english: Women may say we have to get a grip, get on our feet and just let ourselves go!

sentences.english: Easier said than done.

sentences.chinese: 但有帮助的是一个拥挤的舞池，人多就有安全感。

sentences.english: And according to the survey, many men need a drink.

sentences.english: One man questioned said, "I don't think I'm very good at it and therefore need some Dutch courage to get me on the floor."
sentences.chinese: 一位接受调查的男士说：“我觉得我不太擅长跳舞，所以需要酒后之勇（Dutch courage）才能让我走上舞池。”

title: Should schoolchildren have jobs
titleChinese: 中小学生应做兼职工作吗？
paragraphs: When you were at school, the last thing you probably wanted to do was spend your weekends going to work. There was homework to do, sport to play and fun to be had. But our parents probably persuaded us to find a job to earn some money and get some life experience. When I was a teenager I had a paper round: delivering newspapers to people's homes. I then progressed to a Saturday job in a supermarket: stacking shelves and working at the checkout.

Today in the UK you are allowed to work from the age of 13, and many children do take up part-time jobs. It's one of those things that is seen almost as a rite of passage. It's a taste of independence and sometimes a useful thing to put on your CV. Teenagers agree that it teaches valuable lessons about working with adults and also about managing your money. So, that's no bad thing!

Some research has shown that not taking on a Saturday or holiday job could be detrimental to a person later on. A 2015 study by the UK Commission on Employment and Skills found that not participating in part-time work at school age had been blamed by employers' organisations for young adults being ill-prepared for full-time employment. But despite this, recent statistics have shown that the number of schoolchildren in the UK with a part-time job has fallen by a fifth in the past five years.

So, does this mean that British teenagers are now more afraid of hard graft? Probably not. Some experts feel that young people feel going out to work will hinder their performance at school, and they are under more pressure now to study hard and get good exam results - and a good job in the long term. However, Geoff Barton, general secretary of the Association of School and College Leaders, told BBC News that "Properly regulated part-time work is a good way of helping young people learn skills that they will need in their working lives." In reality, it's all about getting the right balance between doing part-time work and having enough time to study and rest.

Many young people actually want to work because it gives them a sense of freedom. One 13 year-old girl called Rachel, who has a Saturday job in a shop, told the BBC that "I enjoy my job because I'm earning money and it helps my confidence speaking to people and socialising with people I work with." That seems like something worth getting up for on a Saturday morning. Did you do a part-time job when you were at school?

title: Paying more for ethical coffee
titleChinese: 付高价喝一杯“道德”咖啡
paragraphs: Do you like to start your day with a cup of joe? Well, you wouldn’t be alone. Millions of people from all over the world brew a cup of coffee first thing in the morning, or at any time of day, for that matter. Do you make it yourself, using instant coffee? Or, if you are a coffee connoisseur, perhaps you use freshly ground beans. Do you take it straight? With a dash of milk? Or maybe even some chocolate sprinkles? Or, failing all of that, maybe you’d rather pay a barista in a cafe to whip one up for you.

Cafes are everywhere these days, offering as many varieties of coffee as there are ways to have it served. And this leads to a range of prices, from cheap grab-and-go coffee, to the ultra-expensive artisanal coffee. However, an increasing number of Western consumers are happy to pay a little over the odds for their cup in order to ensure that it comes from an ethically produced and sustainable source.

At The Attendant, a cafe in east London, staff attempt to make customers aware of the story of the beans that they are drinking and the impact they are having by choosing to drink ethically. For a start, it can make coffee farmers up to three-and-a-half times better off, according to figures from the UN’s World Intellectual Property Organisation (Wipo).

Ryan de Oliveria, The Attendant's co-founder and chief executive, says the extra income allows farmers and their families to have a better quality of life. It also makes investing or reinvesting in their business possible.

Wipo’s figures show smarter processing, branding and marketing make a huge difference to the growers and their communities. Technology now means that the beans can be tracked all the way from the farm to the cup. The research shows that for a pound (454g) of beans going to a supermarket, the export price is $1.45. Most of this goes to the farmer. The price almost doubles when the beans are headed for large western coffee chains. But farmers exporting their beans to artisanal cafes make over $5 per pound. That's because the coffee aficionados who frequent these places are happy to pay more.

It seems that it’s a win-win situation for the farmers, cafes and consumers. So much so that more established coffee businesses are jumping on the band wagon by buying up artisanal rivals who have already embraced this way of doing things. If that’s the case, then the future of coffee production looks a little fairer for all. And that’s something that should get anyone up on the right side of bed.

sentences.english: Do you like to start your day with a cup of joe?

sentences.english: Well, you wouldn’t be alone.
sentences.chinese: 嗯，你不是一个人。

sentences.english: Millions of people from all over the world brew a cup of coffee first thing in the morning, or at any time of day, for that matter.
sentences.chinese: 世界各地数以百万计的人早上的第一件事就是冲泡（brew）一杯咖啡，或者在一天中的任何时候来上一杯。

sentences.english: Do you make it yourself, using instant coffee?
sentences.chinese: 你是自己冲泡速溶咖啡吗？

sentences.english: Or, if you are a coffee connoisseur, perhaps you use freshly ground beans.
sentences.chinese: 或者，如果你是一位咖啡行家（connoisseur），也许你会用现磨的咖啡豆。

sentences.english: Do you take it straight?
sentences.chinese: 你会直接喝纯咖啡吗？

sentences.english: With a dash of milk?
sentences.chinese: 还是加少许牛奶？

sentences.english: Or maybe even some chocolate sprinkles?
sentences.chinese: 或者甚至撒上一些巧克力屑（sprinkles）呢？

sentences.english: Or, failing all of that, maybe you’d rather pay a barista in a cafe to whip one up for you.
sentences.chinese: 或者，如果这些都不喜欢，也许你更愿意付钱给咖啡馆的咖啡师（barista），让他为你快速制作一杯。

sentences.english: Cafes are everywhere these days, offering as many varieties of coffee as there are ways to have it served.
sentences.chinese: 如今咖啡馆无处不在，提供的咖啡种类与供应方式同样多种多样。

sentences.english: And this leads to a range of prices, from cheap grab-and-go coffee, to the ultra-expensive artisanal coffee.
sentences.chinese: 这就导致了咖啡价格的差异，从便宜的即买即走的咖啡，到极其昂贵的手工制作的（artisanal）咖啡。

sentences.english: However, an increasing number of Western consumers are happy to pay a little over the odds for their cup in order to ensure that it comes from an ethically produced and sustainable source.
sentences.chinese: 然而，越来越多的西方消费者乐于为他们的咖啡多（超过正常数量或价格）付一点钱，以便确保咖啡来自符合道德规范且可持续生产的源头。

sentences.english: At The Attendant, a cafe in east London, staff attempt to make customers aware of the story of the beans that they are drinking and the impact they are having by choosing to drink ethically.
sentences.chinese: 在伦敦东部的一家名为“服务员”（The Attendant）的咖啡馆里，员工们试图让顾客了解他们所喝的咖啡豆的故事，以及他们选择符合道德规范的咖啡所产生的影响。

sentences.english: For a start, it can make coffee farmers up to three-and-a-half times better off, according to figures from the UN’s World Intellectual Property Organisation (Wipo).
sentences.chinese: 首先，根据联合国世界知识产权组织（Wipo）的数据，这可以使咖啡农的收入提高多达三倍半。

sentences.english: Ryan de Oliveria, The Attendant's co-founder and chief executive, says the extra income allows farmers and their families to have a better quality of life.
sentences.chinese: “服务员”咖啡馆的联合创始人兼首席执行官瑞安・德奥利维拉（Ryan de Oliveria）表示，额外的收入使农民及其家人能够过上更好的生活质量。

sentences.english: It also makes investing or reinvesting in their business possible.
sentences.chinese: 这也使他们在自己的生意上进行投资或再投资成为可能。

sentences.english: Wipo’s figures show smarter processing, branding and marketing make a huge difference to the growers and their communities.
sentences.chinese: 世界知识产权组织（Wipo）的数据显示，更智能的加工、品牌打造和市场营销对种植者及其所在社区产生了巨大的影响。

sentences.english: Technology now means that the beans can be tracked all the way from the farm to the cup.
sentences.chinese: 如今的技术意味着咖啡豆从农场到杯子的整个过程都可以被追踪。

sentences.english: The research shows that for a pound (454g) of beans going to a supermarket, the export price is $1.45.
sentences.chinese: 研究表明，一磅（454克）运往超市的咖啡豆，出口价格是1.45美元。

sentences.english: Most of this goes to the farmer.
sentences.chinese: 其中大部分收入归农民所有。

sentences.english: The price almost doubles when the beans are headed for large western coffee chains.
sentences.chinese: 当这些咖啡豆运往西方大型咖啡连锁店时，价格几乎翻倍。

sentences.english: But farmers exporting their beans to artisanal cafes make over $5 per pound.
sentences.chinese: 但是，将咖啡豆出口到手工咖啡馆的农民每磅能赚5美元以上。

sentences.english: That's because the coffee aficionados who frequent these places are happy to pay more.
sentences.chinese: 这是因为经常光顾这些地方的咖啡爱好者（aficionados）乐于支付更高的价格。

sentences.english: It seems that it’s a win-win situation for the farmers, cafes and consumers.
sentences.chinese: 看来这对农民、咖啡馆和消费者来说是一个双赢的局面。

sentences.english: So much so that more established coffee businesses are jumping on the band wagon by buying up artisanal rivals who have already embraced this way of doing things.
sentences.chinese: 以至于更多知名的咖啡企业也开始跟风随大流，收购那些已经采用这种经营方式的手工咖啡竞争对手。

sentences.english: If that’s the case, then the future of coffee production looks a little fairer for all.
sentences.chinese: 如果是这样的话，那么咖啡生产的未来对所有人来说似乎都更公平了一些。

sentences.english: And that’s something that should get anyone up on the right side of bed.
sentences.chinese: 而这是一件能让任何人心情愉悦的事情。

title: Is too much screen time affecting children's eyesight
titleChinese: 长时间看屏幕会影响孩子的视力？
paragraphs: These days there is so much tempting technology to look at: smartphones, tablets, computer games and TV screens. Much of our entertainment and education comes from using them, so it's no wonder we spend so much time staring at them. But even if the saying that looking at a screen for too long gives you square eyes isn't true, there is still some concern that it can affect your eyesight. So, should we be worried?

Certainly for children who spend hours glued to a screen there is a concern that their health might be at risk. The lack of physical activity can lead to an increase in their weight. But there is a fear that their eyesight is deteriorating too. Although there's not much evidence to prove this yet, recent findings have opened our eyes to the issue.

Katherine Sellgren from BBC News spoke to Chris Hammond, professor of ophthalmology at King's College London and consultant ophthalmic surgeon at St Thomas' Hospital. He said "We know that myopia, or short-sightedness, is becoming more common… It has reached epidemic levels in East Asia, Singapore, Taiwan, South Korea, where approaching 90% of 18-year-olds are now short-sighted."

But can this be linked to children's obsession with using electronic gadgets? Annegret Dahlmann-Noor, consultant ophthalmologist at Moorfields Eye Hospital in London says lack of natural light seems to be the key issue. She's suggested that children in East Asia study a lot, using computers, smartphones or tablets, and they are go outside less, which could be a cause of short-sightedness. Wearing glasses is one solution, but it's not ideal.

This leads to a dilemma: achieving short-term academic success or protecting your long-term eyesight. It's always going to be a challenge to drag children away from their screens and it's likely that more and more studying will be done online, through a screen. But despite that, Professor Hammond says, "in countries like urban China, where 10% of children in each class per year are becoming short-sighted from about the age of six, there's an argument for saying we should be trying to prevent it." It's evidence we can't turn a blind eye to. So, maybe it's time to hit the 'off' button and get our children outside?

title: Virtual exercise in the gym
titleChinese: 利用虚拟现实技术的新健身体验
paragraphs: Going to the gym can be something that many people find a gruelling experience. It takes time and effort, it often hurts, and it can be extremely tedious. Most weight-related exercises are a combination of sets and reps. In order to see any significant change from any one exercise, it will probably need to be repeated six to eight times, for a minimum of three sets, for about three months. Then there's cardio. For some, there's nothing more boring than endless miles spent running on a treadmill.
But what if there were a way to alleviate the boredom of exercise while still getting a good work out? Luckily for us, there’s virtual reality.

In the past, “playing video games was a sedentary experience,” says Jo Stauffer of the VR Health Institute, “but VR changes all of that". He says that the room-scale experience engages your body in full.

Many VR games are played while standing. In order to play properly, the player is forced to move around swinging their arms or using their legs. After an hour of this on a regular enough basis, it’s not surprising that many people unexpectedly find themselves a little fitter. There are already a number of virtual reality games which, deliberately or not, result in their player ‘getting a good sweat on’ if played for enough time. For example, there’s a first person shooter which forces the player to sidestep, duck and dodge incoming projectiles. That’s cardio. Or there’s a music game which forces players to shadowbox in order to hit the notes – that’s an upper-body workout.

The potential for VR to help people get fit has been noticed by one company. They want to take the whole experience into the gym. They are making a bespoke resistance machine, designed to be used in combination with a VR headset. Players challenge a virtual opponent in a series of games, which results in a 30-minute full-body work out. However, the cost of the equipment is expensive and there are safety concerns to be worked out, says J P Gownder from the consultancy Forrester. So don’t hang up your gym shorts just yet.

Although it’s early days, for those of us who struggle to overcome the tedium of exercise, a new solution could be coming. And a world where a person can exercise and have fun at the same time might be something that many people would want – virtual or not.

title: A lack of women in science
titleChinese: 科学领域缺少女性工作者
paragraphs: There's an old riddle used by psychologists which shows the gender bias people have when it comes to the types of jobs men and women do. Let's see if you can do it: A father and son are in an accident. The father dies. The surgeon refuses to operate on the injured boy saying, "The boy is my son." Can you explain?
According to research done in 2012 by Mikaela Wapman and Deborah Belle at the University of Boston, only 14% of those surveyed were able to imagine that a surgeon could be a woman.

Stereotypes about who should do what type of job are mirrored in the makeup of the workforce. For example, the BBC recently reported that only 10% of UK engineers are women. That's the lowest in Europe, where most other countries put the figure at around 20%. That’s still only a fifth. And it’s not just engineering either. In August 2017, Prof Polly Arnold of Edinburgh University found that only 10% of the top jobs in Scottish science, technology, engineering and mathematics are held by women.

So why is it that women don't go into scientific jobs? Sophie, a girl from a school in Hertfordshire, England, who studied engineering at secondary school, says, "It starts at a young age… girls are put in a corner with a doll while boys play with trucks and cars."

There's also the lack of female role models. “I don’t think they get as much visibility as they deserve,” says Priyanka Dhopade, one of the Women’s Engineering Society top 50 under-35 women engineers. She says that it would make a huge difference for young girls to have someone to look up to and say ‘I want to be like her.’

Regardless of their lack of visibility, a number of pioneering women have paved the way to amazing discoveries. Let us not forget Marie Curie, whose groundbreaking work made her the first Nobel Prize winner in two different fields: physics and chemistry. There's Rajaa Cherkaoui El Moursli, who overcame any number of cultural prejudices to play a key role in the discovery of the Higgs-Boson particle. And Soyeon Yi, who became the first South Korean astronaut in 2008, and who hoped her success would inspire more women.

Quite clearly, women have made momentous contributions to science, technology and engineering. If these achievements were more celebrated, it may encourage girls and young women to consider science as their future career. And as more women start to do these jobs, more people might instantly recognise that the surgeon in the riddle is a woman.

sentences.english: There's an old riddle used by psychologists which shows the gender bias people have when it comes to the types of jobs men and women do.
sentences.chinese: 有一个被心理学家使用的古老谜题，它展示了人们在涉及男性和女性所从事的工作类型时存在的性别偏见（gender bias）。

sentences.english: Let's see if you can do it: A father and son are in an accident.
sentences.chinese: 我们来看看你能否解开它：一对父子遭遇了一场事故。

sentences.english: The father dies.
sentences.chinese: 父亲去世了。

sentences.english: The surgeon refuses to operate on the injured boy saying, "The boy is my son."
sentences.chinese: 外科医生（surgeon）拒绝为受伤的男孩做手术，说道：“这个男孩是我的儿子。”

sentences.english: Can you explain?
sentences.chinese: 你能解释这是怎么回事吗？

sentences.english: According to research done in 2012 by Mikaela Wapman and Deborah Belle at the University of Boston, only 14% of those surveyed were able to imagine that a surgeon could be a woman.
sentences.chinese: 根据波士顿大学（University of Boston）的米凯拉・瓦普曼（Mikaela Wapman）和黛博拉・贝尔（Deborah Belle）在2012年所做的研究，在接受调查的人中，只有14%的人能够想到外科医生可能是女性。

sentences.english: Stereotypes about who should do what type of job are mirrored in the makeup of the workforce.
sentences.chinese: 关于谁应该从事何种工作的刻板印象（Stereotypes）在劳动人口构成中有所体现。

sentences.english: For example, the BBC recently reported that only 10% of UK engineers are women.
sentences.chinese: 例如，BBC最近报道称，英国的工程师中只有10%是女性。

sentences.english: That's the lowest in Europe, where most other countries put the figure at around 20%.
sentences.chinese: 这在欧洲是比例最低的，在大多数其他欧洲国家中，这一比例约为20%。

sentences.english: That’s still only a fifth.
sentences.chinese: 即便如此也仅仅是五分之一。

sentences.english: And it’s not just engineering either.
sentences.chinese: 而且也不只是工程领域如此。

sentences.english: In August 2017, Prof Polly Arnold of Edinburgh University found that only 10% of the top jobs in Scottish science, technology, engineering and mathematics are held by women.
sentences.chinese: 2017年8月，爱丁堡大学（University of Edinburgh）的波莉・阿诺德（Polly Arnold）教授发现，在苏格兰科学、技术、工程和数学领域的高级职位中，只有10%由女性担任。

sentences.english: So why is it that women don't go into scientific jobs?
sentences.chinese: 那么，为什么女性不从事科学领域的工作呢？

sentences.english: Sophie, a girl from a school in Hertfordshire, England, who studied engineering at secondary school, says, "It starts at a young age… girls are put in a corner with a doll while boys play with trucks and cars."
sentences.chinese: 索菲（Sophie）是一名来自英国赫特福德郡（Hertfordshire）一所学校的女孩，她在中学时学习工程专业，她说：“这种情况从小就开始了……当男孩们玩卡车和汽车时，女孩们却被安排在角落里玩洋娃娃。”

sentences.english: There's also the lack of female role models.
sentences.chinese: 还存在缺乏女性榜样（role models）的问题。

sentences.english: “I don’t think they get as much visibility as they deserve,” says Priyanka Dhopade, one of the Women’s Engineering Society top 50 under-35 women engineers.
sentences.chinese: “我认为她们没有得到应有的曝光度（visibility），”普里扬卡・多帕德（Priyanka Dhopade）说道，她是女性工程协会（Women’s Engineering Society）评选出的35岁以下50位杰出女工程师之一。

sentences.english: She says that it would make a huge difference for young girls to have someone to look up to and say ‘I want to be like her.’
sentences.chinese: 她说，对于年轻女孩来说，有一个值得敬仰并说出“我想成为像她那样的人”的人会对她产生巨大的影响。

sentences.english: Regardless of their lack of visibility, a number of pioneering women have paved the way to amazing discoveries.
sentences.chinese: 尽管她们缺乏曝光度，但许多先驱女性为惊人的发现铺平了道路（paved the way）。

sentences.english: Let us not forget Marie Curie, whose groundbreaking work made her the first Nobel Prize winner in two different fields: physics and chemistry.
sentences.chinese: 我们不要忘记玛丽・居里（Marie Curie），她开创性的（groundbreaking）工作使她成为在两个不同领域（物理学和化学）获得诺贝尔奖的第一人。

sentences.english: There's Rajaa Cherkaoui El Moursli, who overcame any number of cultural prejudices to play a key role in the discovery of the Higgs-Boson particle.
sentences.chinese: 还有拉贾・切尔卡维・埃尔・穆尔斯利（Rajaa Cherkaoui El Moursli），她战胜了诸多文化偏见，在希格斯玻色子的发现中发挥了关键作用。

sentences.english: And Soyeon Yi, who became the first South Korean astronaut in 2008, and who hoped her success would inspire more women.
sentences.chinese: 以及李素妍（Soyeon Yi），她在2008年成为了首位韩国女宇航员，并且她希望自己的成功能够激励更多的女性。

sentences.english: Quite clearly, women have made momentous contributions to science, technology and engineering.
sentences.chinese: 很明显，女性对科学、技术和工程做出了重大的（momentous）贡献。

sentences.english: If these achievements were more celebrated, it may encourage girls and young women to consider science as their future career.
sentences.chinese: 如果这些成就能够得到更多的赞誉，这可能会鼓励女孩和年轻女性将科学领域视为她们未来的职业。

sentences.english: And as more women start to do these jobs, more people might instantly recognise that the surgeon in the riddle is a woman.
sentences.chinese: 而且随着越来越多的女性开始从事这些工作，更多的人可能会立刻意识到那个谜题中的外科医生是一位女性。

title: Millennial grooms take spouse’s name
titleChinese: 千禧一代新郎选择婚后随妻姓
paragraphs: No one knows how long humans have been giving themselves names, but one thing is sure: surnames are a much more recent idea than given names. In Europe, surnames were developed to distinguish between individuals who had the same moniker. They were brought to the UK by the French nobility following the Norman Conquest around the 12th century and became common around the 14th century.

Another tradition that the Normans introduced was that of coverture. This was a law which said that a woman became a man's property when they got married. In those days, only a man could be the head of the family and allowed to own property. At this point the bride lost her maiden name. Over time, this has led to the tradition that upon marriage a woman relinquishes her maiden name and takes on her new husband’s family name.

Fast forward to the present. These days a woman choosing not to change her name to match her husband’s after marriage has long been a norm. The first recorded case is widely believed to be an American suffragette called Lucy Stone. When she got married in 1855, she refused to take her husband's name. After that, other ideas such as merging and double-barrelling also became common.

However, it would seem that a new trend is arising. One in ten millennial males is now electing to replace their surname with their wife’s. That's according to a recent study of 2000 UK adults by Opinium, a strategic insight agency. In a BBC article, Rory Dearlove née Cook, explained that for him it wasn’t important to keep his surname. He thought it would be nice for his wife and him to have the same last name. The bride, Lucy, had made it clear before getting married that she had no intention of changing hers, but thought that he would keep his too. “He's entitled to keep his just as I am entitled to keep mine,” she commented.

Other men had different reasons. Charlie Shaw, dubbed 'Morley' at birth, explained that it was, “a gesture of allegiance and an opportunity to acknowledge the unseen patriarchal bias and sexism in our society.” It’s worth noting that, in the UK at least, only the fathers of the couple being married are on the marriage certificate. The mothers do not appear at all.

However, not everyone is in favour of altering tradition. Rachel Robnett, a researcher at the University of Nevada, surveyed a number of people in the US and UK and found that a man whose wife keeps her maiden name is viewed as ‘feminine’, while the woman was believed to ‘wear the trousers’. And when one family found out that their son was to take his wife’s name, they refused to attend the wedding. To them it was proof that he was totally under the thumb.

‘What’s in a name?’ Shakespeare asked in Romeo and Juliet. It would seem, depending on who you talk to, a great deal. Whether maintaining traditional naming conventions, keeping the surname, or swapping names, these days at least there is a choice to be made.

sentences.english: No one knows how long humans have been giving themselves names, but one thing is sure: surnames are a much more recent idea than given names.

sentences.english: In Europe, surnames were developed to distinguish between individuals who had the same moniker.
sentences.chinese: 在欧洲，姓氏的产生是为了区分（distinguish）那些有相同名字（moniker）的人。

sentences.english: They were brought to the UK by the French nobility following the Norman Conquest around the 12th century and became common around the 14th century.
sentences.chinese: 大约在12世纪诺曼征服之后，法国贵族将姓氏带到了英国，并在14世纪左右变得普遍起来。

sentences.english: Another tradition that the Normans introduced was that of coverture.
sentences.chinese: 诺曼人引入的另一个传统是夫权制。

sentences.english: This was a law which said that a woman became a man's property when they got married.
sentences.chinese: 这是一项法律，规定女人在结婚后就成为男人的财产。

sentences.english: In those days, only a man could be the head of the family and allowed to own property.
sentences.chinese: 在那个时候，只有男人可以成为一家之主并被允许拥有财产。

sentences.english: At this point the bride lost her maiden name.
sentences.chinese: 此时，新娘失去了她的娘家姓。

sentences.english: Over time, this has led to the tradition that upon marriage a woman relinquishes her maiden name and takes on her new husband’s family name.
sentences.chinese: 随着时间的推移，这就形成了一种传统，即女人在结婚时会放弃（relinquishes）娘家姓，改用她新婚丈夫的姓氏。

sentences.english: Fast forward to the present.
sentences.chinese: 快进到现在。

sentences.english: These days a woman choosing not to change her name to match her husband’s after marriage has long been a norm.
sentences.chinese: 如今，女人在婚后选择不随丈夫姓早已成为一种常态。

sentences.english: The first recorded case is widely believed to be an American suffragette called Lucy Stone.
sentences.chinese: 人们普遍认为，第一个有记录的案例是一位名叫露西・斯通（Lucy Stone）的美国妇女参政论者。

sentences.english: When she got married in 1855, she refused to take her husband's name.
sentences.chinese: 1855年她结婚时，拒绝随丈夫姓。

sentences.english: After that, other ideas such as merging and double-barrelling also became common.
sentences.chinese: 在那之后，其他的做法，比如合并姓氏（merging）和采用双姓（double-barrelling）也变得常见起来。

sentences.english: However, it would seem that a new trend is arising.
sentences.chinese: 然而，似乎出现了一种新的趋势。

sentences.english: One in ten millennial males is now electing to replace their surname with their wife’s. That's according to a recent study of 2000 UK adults by Opinium, a strategic insight agency.
sentences.chinese: 根据战略洞察机构奥皮尼姆（Opinium）最近对2000名英国成年人的一项研究，现在十分之一的千禧一代男性选择改用他们妻子的姓氏。

sentences.english: In a BBC article, Rory Dearlove née Cook, explained that for him it wasn’t important to keep his surname.
sentences.chinese: 在BBC的一篇文章中，罗里・迪尔洛夫，原姓库克，解释道，对他来说，保留自己的姓氏并不重要。

sentences.english: He thought it would be nice for his wife and him to have the same last name.
sentences.chinese: 他认为他和妻子有相同的姓氏会很好。

sentences.english: The bride, Lucy, had made it clear before getting married that she had no intention of changing hers, but thought that he would keep his too.
sentences.chinese: 新娘露西在结婚前就明确表示她无意更改自己的姓氏，但她认为他也会保留自己的姓氏。

sentences.english: “He's entitled to keep his just as I am entitled to keep mine,” she commented.
sentences.chinese: “他有权保留他的姓氏，就像我有权保留我的一样，”她评论道。

sentences.english: Other men had different reasons.
sentences.chinese: 其他男性有不同的原因。

sentences.english: Charlie Shaw, dubbed 'Morley' at birth, explained that it was, “a gesture of allegiance and an opportunity to acknowledge the unseen patriarchal bias and sexism in our society.”
sentences.chinese: 查理・肖（Charlie Shaw），出生时被称为（dubbed）“莫利（Morley）”，他解释说，这是“一种表示忠诚（allegiance）的姿态，也是一个承认我们社会中无形的父权制（patriarchal）偏见和性别歧视（sexism）的机会。”

sentences.english: It’s worth noting that, in the UK at least, only the fathers of the couple being married are on the marriage certificate.
sentences.chinese: 值得注意的是，至少在英国，结婚证上只有结婚双方的父亲的名字。

sentences.english: The mothers do not appear at all.
sentences.chinese: 母亲的名字根本不会出现。

sentences.english: However, not everyone is in favour of altering tradition.
sentences.chinese: 然而，并不是每个人都赞成改变传统。

sentences.english: Rachel Robnett, a researcher at the University of Nevada, surveyed a number of people in the US and UK and found that a man whose wife keeps her maiden name is viewed as ‘feminine’, while the woman was believed to ‘wear the trousers’.
sentences.chinese: 内华达大学（University of Nevada）的研究员瑞秋・罗布内特（Rachel Robnett）对美国和英国的一些人进行了调查，发现妻子保留娘家姓的男人会被认为很“女性化”，而女人则被认为是“当家作主”。

sentences.english: And when one family found out that their son was to take his wife’s name, they refused to attend the wedding.
sentences.chinese: 当一个家庭发现他们的儿子要改用妻子的姓氏时，他们拒绝参加婚礼。

sentences.english: To them it was proof that he was totally under the thumb.
sentences.chinese: 对他们来说，这证明他受制于人（under the thumb）。

sentences.english: ‘What’s in a name?’
sentences.chinese: “名字里包含着什么呢？”

sentences.english: Shakespeare asked in Romeo and Juliet.
sentences.chinese: 莎士比亚在《罗密欧与朱丽叶》（Romeo and Juliet）中问道。

sentences.english: It would seem, depending on who you talk to, a great deal.
sentences.chinese: 似乎，这取决于你和谁交谈，意义可能大不相同。

sentences.english: Whether maintaining traditional naming conventions, keeping the surname, or swapping names, these days at least there is a choice to be made.
sentences.chinese: 无论是遵循传统的命名习俗，保留姓氏，还是交换姓氏，至少如今人们有了可以选择的机会。

title: Why stress makes you fat
titleChinese: 压力为什么能让你变胖？
paragraphs: Have you ever had a stressful day? Many people do in the course of their daily lives. And on these high-pressure days, they might find themselves reaching for a sugary snack. Perhaps this is part of their daily routine. Or perhaps on this particular day, their self-control is a bit low and they feel compelled to take a sugar hit.

Stress is natural. That feeling of strain or pressure is a biological response, and under the right circumstances can be a great source of motivation. However, too much stress, especially chronic stress, has been linked to sleep disruption, a higher likelihood of a stroke, heart-attack, ulcer or depression, among other things. But why should stress make a person comfort eat?

Dr Giles Yeo, a member of the BBC’s Trust Me, I’m a Doctor team, got together with scientists from Leeds University to conduct an experiment into the effect of stress on blood sugar. Dr Yeo was subjected to a stress test. In the first stage, he was forced to answer mathematical questions rapidly. In the second, he had to immerse his hand in a bath of ice-cold water for a period of time.

Before and after these tests, the Leeds scientists would measure Dr Yeo’s blood sugar levels. These are the levels which rise when we eat as our body takes in the energy of the food. In a healthy person, these levels quickly return to normal. However, when Dr Yeo was being deliberately subjected to stress, his blood sugar took six times longer to drop than on a stress-free day.

When we become stressed, our bodies enter ‘fight or flight’ mode. Because our body believes it’s under attack, it releases glucose into the blood to provide energy for muscles. However, if we don’t use that energy, our body then releases insulin to make the blood sugar levels drop. This drop causes a hunger response: you want to eat. And what you particularly crave is sugary food, which rapidly replenishes the energy you have lost. If this happens repeatedly, over a long enough period of time, these high-calorie foods can lead to obesity.

So what can we do to combat the stress? In an article for the BBC, Dr Michael Mosley recommends ‘stress-busting’ techniques, like exercise, gardening, mindfulness or another activities that you enjoy. But his strongest recommendation is trying to get a good night’s sleep. A recent study carried out by researchers at King's College, London found that if you deprived people of sleep, they would consume, on average, an extra 385kcal per day, which is equivalent to the calories in a large muffin. So, try sleeping to decrease stress, and as a result make it easier to keep yourself a little trimmer.

title: How late is too late
titleChinese: 多晚算太晚？
paragraphs: Time flies, or so they say. No matter where you are, humans are constantly measuring and checking time. Some of us are good at it – planning and doing things way ahead of time - while others are always trying to beat the clock and do things at the eleventh hour. And that’s only if you’re on time. What about if you are behind time?

Tardiness can be serious. If you were one minute late for work, would you resign? It may sound extreme to many of us, but that is exactly what occurred in the UK upper chamber of parliament, the House of Lords, in January 2018. International development minister Lord Bates arrived one minute late, and, as a result, was unable to answer a scheduled question. Instead of trying to make up for lost time, as many might do, he resigned on the spot. He apologised for his discourtesy and stated that he was ashamed. His resignation, though, was not accepted by the UK prime minister.

So, how late is too late? Many cultures take punctuality very seriously, whereas others seem to accept lagging behind as just the normal way of things. Members of the BBC from various different cultures were asked about the concept of timekeeping in their native countries and responded with a raft of answers.

BBC employees from Latin America, Rwanda and Sri Lanka said that there are more flexible attitudes to timekeeping in their cultures. In Latin America, things may happen five minutes, 20 minutes, an hour or even two after they were planned. Whereas, in Sri Lanka, lateness is a part of the daily routine. This is because of poor infrastructure and heavy traffic conditions. In Rwanda, those who attend to deadlines with rigid timekeeping are said to be ‘like a typical European’. This is in a place where it is not unusual to arrive at 11am for a meeting which started at nine.

On the other hand, German and Japanese employees mentioned a stricter adherence to time. In Japan, it is common to make an effort to arrive with time to spare for an appointment. Those who arrived at the stroke of nine to a meeting starting at nine a.m. would be considered late. In Germany, however, if a dinner party were to begin at eight, a person who had arrived five minutes prior, may walk around the block to ensure that they arrive at eight on the dot.

It seems that the answer is subjective, and what is considered acceptable is based on culture. That said, if you don’t mind waiting, it might be best to attend your appointments in good time. And if the worst comes to the worst, remember the old English proverb. Better late than never.

title: The problem with disposable coffee
titleChinese: 外带咖啡纸杯的“回收难题”
paragraphs: Millions of us grab a coffee on our way to work. And when we do, it probably comes served in a branded, disposable, cardboard coffee cup. Once the coffee is done, just pop the cup into a recycling bin and forget about it. The cup will be taken away and turned into a new one for you to use again tomorrow. The system works, right?

There’s a hitch. In the UK, we throw away an estimated 2.5 billion disposable coffee cups every year. And despite being recyclable in theory, in practice only very few of them are dealt with in a way that makes them sustainable. This makes them a bit of an obstacle. What throws a spanner in the works is the layer of polyethylene that makes the cup waterproof, and the lid, which is most often made of polystyrene. As a result, most of the cups end up in landfill.

But there are efforts underway to tackle this issue. One company, Biome Bioplastics, has come up with a fully compostable, recyclable cup that uses natural materials, such as potato starch, as waterproofing. Mr Mines, its chief executive, believes that this is the first time bioplastic has been used for disposable cups and lids that have to cope with hot liquid. And they're still fully recyclable.

Another feasible solution has been proposed by Frugalpac, who have patented a cup with a lightly-attached plastic lining. This can be easily separated during the recycling and ‘offers a more pragmatic solution’ than changing our current recycling habits, says Frugalpac’s founder Martin Myerscough.

Safia Qureshi says India has provided the inspiration for her solution. She puts forward that we use returnable and reusable cups, which are tracked and collected by her company Cup Club. They will be responsible for collecting, washing and redistributing the clean cups to participating retailers.

One final example of lateral thinking comes from Cupffee. This trio from Bulgaria have combined cereals to form a cup which can be eaten once the drink is finished. It is apparently sweet and crisp, can hold a coffee for up to 40 minutes and will biodegrade within weeks.

Whether any of these innovative ideas are a perfect fit for this disposable issue, only time will tell. It’s possible that a more viable solution has yet to be ventured, though it may not be long in coming. All it may require is a little more thinking outside the box… or should that be coffee cup?

title: What you didn't know about the verges of sleep
titleChinese: 你不知道的“入睡边缘”常识
paragraphs: How long does it take you to fall asleep? Are you out like a light as soon as your head hits the pillow, or does it take you more than a little time to doze off?

If the average night’s sleep is eight hours, or a third of a day, then it means we spend around one third of our lives in this dormant state. Science already has reams of data on the brain’s activity during sleep itself. Now, an international group of researchers at the University of Cambridge are researching that dopey state we all go through between wide awake and fast asleep.

This transitional period usually lasts between five and 20 minutes, says Sridhar Rajan Jagannathan, one of Cambridge’s Gates Scholars. However, people exhibit a variety of behaviour within this time. For some, going to the land of nod is a smooth, quick journey, while others have more difficulty. They “begin to get drowsy” and then snap out of it “back to alertness” he says.

The aim of the research is to find out how this pre-sleep phase, when the eyes glaze, the attention wanders and the mind is lulled, could be linked to accidents and dangerous mistakes. This could happen during the day while at work. “If you’re doing some boring task, you might be drowsy in this period. Small drift-offs can cause big problems,” says Mr Jangannathan. This is not just connected to safety concerns with driving, for example, but any task where concentration and decision making are important.

There are positive sides to this hypnagogic period too. Some experts think there is a connection to creativity and imagination. This is caused by a reduction in your inhibitions, which makes you more creative. You have more freedom to express yourself, and you’re more willing to make mistakes. It certainly seems to support the old adage of sleeping on it to solve a problem.

Ultimately, there are hopes that research into brain activity during falling asleep and waking might help stroke victims who are trying to regain lost physical functions. That could well be a pipe dream. There are also research efforts underway to find ways to warn of the onset of sleep, identifying changes in eye movements or brain activity. These could have practical applications for tired people operating heavy machinery and may help ensure that when it comes to accidents, we’re not caught napping.

sentences.chinese: 如果平均每晚睡眠8小时，也就是一天的三分之一，那么这意味着我们一生中大约有三分之一的时间处于这种休眠的（dormant）状态。

sentences.english: Science already has reams of data on the brain’s activity during sleep itself.
sentences.chinese: 科学领域已经有了大量的（reams of）关于睡眠期间大脑活动的数据。

sentences.english: Now, an international group of researchers at the University of Cambridge are researching that dopey state we all go through between wide awake and fast asleep.
sentences.chinese: 现在，剑桥大学的一个国际研究团队正在研究我们都会经历的从完全清醒到熟睡之间那种昏昏欲睡的（dopey）状态。

sentences.english: This transitional period usually lasts between five and 20 minutes, says Sridhar Rajan Jagannathan, one of Cambridge’s Gates Scholars.
sentences.chinese: 剑桥大学盖茨学者斯里达尔・拉詹・贾甘纳坦（Sridhar Rajan Jagannathan）说，这个过渡阶段通常持续5到20分钟。

sentences.english: However, people exhibit a variety of behaviour within this time.
sentences.chinese: 然而，人们在这段时间内会表现出各种各样的行为。

sentences.english: For some, going to the land of nod is a smooth, quick journey, while others have more difficulty.
sentences.chinese: 对有些人来说，进入梦乡（the land of nod）是一个顺畅、快速的过程，而另一些人则更困难。

sentences.english: They “begin to get drowsy” and then snap out of it “back to alertness” he says.
sentences.chinese: 他说，他们“开始变得昏昏欲睡（drowsy）”，然后又突然清醒过来“恢复警觉”。

sentences.english: The aim of the research is to find out how this pre-sleep phase, when the eyes glaze, the attention wanders and the mind is lulled, could be linked to accidents and dangerous mistakes.
sentences.chinese: 这项研究的目的是弄清楚，当眼睛变得呆滞（glaze）、注意力分散、大脑平静下来（lulled）时，这个睡前阶段与意外事故和危险失误之间可能存在怎样的联系。

sentences.english: This could happen during the day while at work.
sentences.chinese: 这种情况可能在白天工作时发生。

sentences.english: “If you’re doing some boring task, you might be drowsy in this period.
sentences.chinese: 贾甘纳坦先生说：“如果你在做一些无聊的任务，在这个阶段你可能会昏昏欲睡。

sentences.english: Small drift-offs can cause big problems,” says Mr Jangannathan.
sentences.chinese: 短暂的瞌睡（drift-offs）可能会导致大问题。”

sentences.english: This is not just connected to safety concerns with driving, for example, but any task where concentration and decision making are important.
sentences.chinese: 这不仅仅与例如安全驾驶问题有关，还与任何需要集中注意力和做出决策的任务有关。

sentences.english: There are positive sides to this hypnagogic period too.
sentences.chinese: 这个半梦半醒的（hypnagogic）阶段也有积极的一面。

sentences.english: Some experts think there is a connection to creativity and imagination.
sentences.chinese: 一些专家认为它与创造力和想象力有关。

sentences.english: This is caused by a reduction in your inhibitions, which makes you more creative.
sentences.chinese: 这是由于抑制作用的减弱，这使你更具创造力。

sentences.english: You have more freedom to express yourself, and you’re more willing to make mistakes.
sentences.chinese: 你有更多自由来表达自己，也更愿意犯错。

sentences.english: It certainly seems to support the old adage of sleeping on it to solve a problem.
sentences.chinese: 这似乎确实支持了“把问题留到第二天再解决（sleeping on it）”这句古老的谚语。

sentences.english: Ultimately, there are hopes that research into brain activity during falling asleep and waking might help stroke victims who are trying to regain lost physical functions.
sentences.chinese: 最终，人们希望对入睡和醒来时大脑活动的研究可能会帮助中风患者恢复失去的身体功能。

sentences.english: That could well be a pipe dream.
sentences.chinese: 这很可能只是一个空想（pipe dream）。

sentences.english: There are also research efforts underway to find ways to warn of the onset of sleep, identifying changes in eye movements or brain activity.
sentences.chinese: 目前也正在进行研究，试图找到方法来预警睡眠的开始，识别眼球运动或大脑活动的变化。

sentences.english: These could have practical applications for tired people operating heavy machinery and may help ensure that when it comes to accidents, we’re not caught napping.
sentences.chinese: 这些研究对于操作重型机械的疲劳人群可能有实际应用，并且可能有助于确保在事故发生时，我们不会措手不及（caught napping）。

title: App to reward non-use of phone
titleChinese: 放下手机就可积分换奖励
paragraphs: We’re all probably guilty of using our phones a little too often. With the rise of the mobile phone, and later the smartphone, access to communication and information has never been so convenient or tempting. Of course, there are those who only pay it any attention when it goes off or sends them an alert. But there are many who find that their phone is a constant distraction.

There's been an abundance of articles recently relating to mobile phone addiction or diversion. In the UK, looking at a mobile phone rather than focussing on the road has been made illegal. Having your attention diverted from driving by a phone carries a stiff penalty. It’s also no coincidence that the word ‘smombie’ has been coined. The word is made up of two: smartphone zombie, and it describes those people who walk around totally captivated by their phone completely unaware of their surroundings.

Smartphone disruption is an issue in schools too. A study by the University of Texas has suggested that just having a smartphone within eyeshot can reduce productivity, slow down response speed and reduce grades, as the eyes of the students keep being drawn away from their work. A second, related study by the London School of Economics has found that students who did not use their smartphones on school grounds saw an increase of 6.4% in test scores.

This issue of productivity and the degree to which smartphones engross young people caused three students from Copenhagen Business school to develop an app to attempt to help combat smartphone fascination. The app, called ‘Hold’, rewards students for time they spend not using the device. For every 20 minutes that a phone is not used between the hours of seven in the morning and 11 at night, its user will accumulate 10 points.

These points can be exchanged for a number of goods and services on the app’s marketplace, with brands such as Caffè Nero, Vue cinemas and Amazon signing up. For example, to earn two free coffees, students will need 300 points. This is the equivalent of 10 hours on the app.

The app has already become the centre of attention in Scandinavia, with more than 120,000 users across Norway, Denmark and Sweden. And soon it will be launched in 170 universities in the UK too. Could the era of people zoning out on reality and only tuning in to their phones be over? As more and more pay heed, it’s certainly possible. And how else are you likely to be rewarded for not paying attention?

title: Will robots cost us our jobs
titleChinese: 机器人会抢走我们的饭碗吗？
paragraphs: As new technology is introduced, there are many who worry about its impact on our current and future lifestyles – particularly when it comes to jobs. It is a current belief that with the rise of robotics and artificial intelligence, many people’s jobs, and therefore their livelihoods, are likely to be lost to automation.

This type of fear isn’t new. In the 19th century, the automated weaving machine was revolutionising the English textiles industry and would contribute to the Industrial Revolution. When manual workers became redundant, it sparked protests at the loss of their vocation.

Automation in the work place is nothing new. Machines have been performing menial tasks on our behalf for years, allowing us to escape the drudgery that accompanies many repetitive jobs. In fact, the International Federation of Robotics states that in manufacturing on average there are now 74 robots per 10,000 employees. That has risen from 66 in 2015.

General Manager of Digital Customer Engagement Solutions at tech firm Nuance, Bernard Louvat, believes that ‘AI is a big threat to low-skilled jobs, no question.’ He also thinks that AI chatbots will oust most call centre staff within a decade. When you consider that a large telecoms company like AT&T employs around 100,000 call centre staff, that’s a lot of people on the dole.

And that’s just one industry. A recent report from the McKinsey Global Institute, a private sector think tank, states that nearly two thirds of all jobs could have at least 30% of their activities automated by 2030.

However, McKinsey also believes that this new technology will also ‘create new occupations that do not exist today, much as technologies in the past have done.’ As the horse gave way to the car, hostlers became mechanics and mechanised manufacturing drove up wages and created more long-term roles than it destroyed. In fact, figures from the World Bank have shown that despite a 2.2 billion rise in population between 1991 and 2017, global unemployment has fallen by 0.3%.

‘It’s an evolution of work’ says Ian Barkin, co-founder of Symphony Ventures, a robotic process automation specialist. As low-skilled jobs are taken on by AI, people will need to learn new skills. ‘This calls on us to focus on up-skilling, Technology can lead to job reductions but it doesn’t have to,’ says Barkin.

Whether or not robotics and AI will leave us all jobless remains to be seen. Current views on the subject are mixed. Increased automation could indeed lead to a loss of some jobs, but at the same time is likely to create many more as new skills are required. Will they balance out? I’ll get my AI assistant to get back to you on that one.

sentences.english: As new technology is introduced, there are many who worry about its impact on our current and future lifestyles – particularly when it comes to jobs.
sentences.chinese: 随着新技术的引入，很多人担心它对我们当前和未来生活方式的影响——尤其是在工作方面。

sentences.english: It is a current belief that with the rise of robotics and artificial intelligence, many people’s jobs, and therefore their livelihoods, are likely to be lost to automation.
sentences.chinese: 目前人们普遍认为，随着机器人技术和人工智能的兴起，许多人的工作，进而他们的生计，可能会因自动化（automation）而丧失。

sentences.english: This type of fear isn’t new.
sentences.chinese: 这种担忧并非新鲜事。

sentences.english: In the 19th century, the automated weaving machine was revolutionising the English textiles industry and would contribute to the Industrial Revolution.
sentences.chinese: 在19世纪，自动织布机彻底改变了英国的纺织业，并促成了工业革命。

sentences.english: When manual workers became redundant, it sparked protests at the loss of their vocation.
sentences.chinese: 当手工工人被裁员（redundant）时，就引发了人们对失去工作（vocation）的抗议。

sentences.english: Automation in the work place is nothing new.
sentences.chinese: 工作场所的自动化并非新鲜事物。

sentences.english: Machines have been performing menial tasks on our behalf for years, allowing us to escape the drudgery that accompanies many repetitive jobs.
sentences.chinese: 多年来，机器一直在替我们执行枯燥琐碎的（menial）任务，使我们得以摆脱许多重复性工作所带来的辛苦乏味的苦差事；单调乏味（drudgery）。

sentences.english: In fact, the International Federation of Robotics states that in manufacturing on average there are now 74 robots per 10,000 employees.
sentences.chinese: 事实上，国际机器人联合会指出，在制造业中，目前平均每10000名员工就有74台机器人。

sentences.english: That has risen from 66 in 2015.
sentences.chinese: 这一数字与2015年66台相比有所上升。

sentences.english: General Manager of Digital Customer Engagement Solutions at tech firm Nuance, Bernard Louvat, believes that ‘AI is a big threat to low-skilled jobs, no question.’
sentences.chinese: 科技公司Nuance的数字客户互动解决方案总经理伯纳德・卢瓦特（Bernard Louvat）认为，“毫无疑问，人工智能对低技能工作来说是一个巨大威胁。”

sentences.english: He also thinks that AI chatbots will oust most call centre staff within a decade.
sentences.chinese: 他还认为，人工智能聊天机器人将在十年内取代（oust）大多数呼叫中心员工。

sentences.english: When you consider that a large telecoms company like AT&T employs around 100,000 call centre staff, that’s a lot of people on the dole.
sentences.chinese: 当你想到像美国电话电报公司（AT&T）这样的大型电信公司雇佣了约10万名呼叫中心员工时，那就意味着会有很多人靠失业救济金生活。

sentences.english: And that’s just one industry.
sentences.chinese: 而这只是一个行业。

sentences.english: A recent report from the McKinsey Global Institute, a private sector think tank, states that nearly two thirds of all jobs could have at least 30% of their activities automated by 2030.
sentences.chinese: 私营企业智库麦肯锡全球研究所（McKinsey Global Institute）最近的一份报告指出，到2030年，几乎三分之二的工作至少有30%的工作内容可以实现自动化。

sentences.english: However, McKinsey also believes that this new technology will also ‘create new occupations that do not exist today, much as technologies in the past have done.’
sentences.chinese: 然而，麦肯锡也认为，这项新技术也会“创造出如今尚不存在的新职业，就像过去的技术所做的那样”。

sentences.english: As the horse gave way to the car, hostlers became mechanics and mechanised manufacturing drove up wages and created more long-term roles than it destroyed.
sentences.chinese: 随着马被汽车取代，马夫（hostlers）变成了机械师，机械化制造业提高了工资水平，创造出的长期岗位比它淘汰的岗位更多。

sentences.english: In fact, figures from the World Bank have shown that despite a 2.2 billion rise in population between 1991 and 2017, global unemployment has fallen by 0.3%.
sentences.chinese: 事实上，世界银行的数据显示，尽管1991年至2017年间人口增加了22亿，但全球失业率却下降了0.3%。

sentences.english: ‘It’s an evolution of work’ says Ian Barkin, co-founder of Symphony Ventures, a robotic process automation specialist.
sentences.chinese: Symphony Ventures的联合创始人，机器人流程自动化专家伊恩・巴金（Ian Barkin）说：“这是工作的一种进化。”

sentences.english: As low-skilled jobs are taken on by AI, people will need to learn new skills.
sentences.chinese: 随着人工智能承担低技能工作，人们将需要学习新技能。

sentences.english: ‘This calls on us to focus on up-skilling, Technology can lead to job reductions but it doesn’t have to,’ says Barkin.
sentences.chinese: 巴金说：“这就要求我们专注于技能提升（up-skilling）。技术可能会导致工作岗位减少，但也并非必然如此。”

sentences.english: Whether or not robotics and AI will leave us all jobless remains to be seen.
sentences.chinese: 机器人技术和人工智能是否会让我们都失业还有待观察。

sentences.english: Current views on the subject are mixed.
sentences.chinese: 目前关于这个问题的观点不一。

sentences.english: Increased automation could indeed lead to a loss of some jobs, but at the same time is likely to create many more as new skills are required.
sentences.chinese: 自动化程度的提高确实可能导致一些工作岗位的流失，但同时，由于需要新技能，也可能会创造出更多的岗位。

sentences.english: Will they balance out?
sentences.chinese: 它们会达到平衡吗？

sentences.english: I’ll get my AI assistant to get back to you on that one.
sentences.chinese: 关于这一点，我会让我的人工智能助手再回复你。

title: Who needs a manbag
titleChinese: 哪类男士会选择“manbag”？
paragraphs: We have so much stuff to carry around these days – mobile phones, keys, credit cards and laptops. Some of us might stuff them into various pockets in our clothes and others will put them in a bag. For women this might be a practical and trendy handbag. But how are men supposed to carry things around and look cool?

The answer is a manbag! They are the height of fashion at the moment – a stylish accessory that modern men are carrying around. I'm a little cynical about these must-have items – let's face it, a manbag by any other name is a bag and I have one - my trusty backpack. However, senior fashion analyst for market research company Mintel, Tamara Senders, describes a manbag as "a bag worn by men, including backpacks and other styles such as shoulder bags." I can't see my old backpack being a style icon, but maybe I'm just not on-trend: According to Mintel, 15 per cent of men bought one in the UK last year.

Maybe it's the name that's putting me off. Why does a bag have to have a gender? I suppose they're being marketed as a stylish fashion item designed to look good on men. I've heard that many big names have flocked to adopt the trend. Pharrell Williams, David Beckham and Kanye West, are just some of those who've been spotted rocking a manbag.

My reservations about being seen carrying one may be down to my Britishness. According to Nick Carvell, the Contributing Fashion Editor for GQ magazine: "In Britain we are still very tied up with that idea of masculinity that is almost so fragile that it can be dented by carrying a bag." So, while some British men might think a manbag to be effeminate and not very 'macho', he thinks that many Europeans don't have an issue with toting such a fashionable item.

Of course, if I was to exchange my old backpack for a manbag, it would come at a price. With people like Louis Vuitton, Fendi, Gucci and Dolce and Gabbana designing these bags, they can come with a hefty price tag. I suppose that's the price of fashion! And apparently, if I had any spare cash, I could complete my designer outfit by buying a murse – that's a man's purse!

I suppose fashions change and we have come a long way from the days when men carried their things in a very masculine briefcase - sturdy, sensible and practical. Now, it seems, we have to put as much thought into buying a bag as we do into buying our clothes.

vocabulary.entry: reservation [ˌrezəˈveɪʃn] n. 保留意见；疑惑；预订；预约；保留地

sentences.english: We have so much stuff to carry around these days – mobile phones, keys, credit cards and laptops.
sentences.chinese: 如今我们有太多东西要随身携带——手机、钥匙、信用卡和笔记本电脑。

sentences.english: Some of us might stuff them into various pockets in our clothes and others will put them in a bag.
sentences.chinese: 我们中的一些人可能会把它们塞进衣服的各个口袋里，而另一些人则会把它们放在包里。

sentences.english: For women this might be a practical and trendy handbag.
sentences.chinese: 对女性来说，这可能是一个实用又时髦的（trendy）手提包。

sentences.english: But how are men supposed to carry things around and look cool?
sentences.chinese: 但男性要怎么携带东西又看起来很酷呢？

sentences.english: The answer is a manbag!
sentences.chinese: 答案是男士包！

sentences.english: They are the height of fashion at the moment – a stylish accessory that modern men are carrying around.
sentences.chinese: 它们目前是最流行的——一种现代男性随身携带的时尚配饰。

sentences.english: I'm a little cynical about these must-have items – let's face it, a manbag by any other name is a bag and I have one - my trusty backpack.
sentences.chinese: 我对这些必备品有点愤世嫉俗（cynical）——面对现实吧，不管叫什么，男士包就是个包，而且我就有一个——我可靠的双肩背包。

sentences.english: However, senior fashion analyst for market research company Mintel, Tamara Senders, describes a manbag as "a bag worn by men, including backpacks and other styles such as shoulder bags."
sentences.chinese: 然而，市场研究公司英敏特（Mintel）的高级时尚分析师塔玛拉・森德斯（Tamara Senders）将男士包描述为“男性背的包，包括背包以及其他款式，如肩包”。

sentences.english: I can't see my old backpack being a style icon, but maybe I'm just not on-trend: According to Mintel, 15 per cent of men bought one in the UK last year.
sentences.chinese: 我不觉得我的旧背包会成为时尚标志，但也许我只是跟不上潮流：据英敏特的数据，去年在英国，15%的男性购买了男士包。

sentences.english: Maybe it's the name that's putting me off.
sentences.chinese: 也许是这个名字让我反感。

sentences.english: Why does a bag have to have a gender?
sentences.chinese: 为什么包还要分性别呢？

sentences.english: I suppose they're being marketed as a stylish fashion item designed to look good on men.
sentences.chinese: 我想它们正在被当作专为男性设计、看起来很有型的时尚单品来推销。

sentences.english: I've heard that many big names have flocked to adopt the trend.
sentences.chinese: 我听说很多名人都热衷于追随这一潮流。

sentences.english: Pharrell Williams, David Beckham and Kanye West, are just some of those who've been spotted rocking a manbag.
sentences.chinese: 法瑞尔・威廉姆斯（Pharrell Williams）、大卫・贝克汉姆（David Beckham）和坎耶・维斯特（Kanye West），只是被看到背男士包名人中的一部分。

sentences.english: My reservations about being seen carrying one may be down to my Britishness.
sentences.chinese: 我对被人看到背着男士包有所顾虑，这可能归因于我是英国人。

sentences.english: According to Nick Carvell, the Contributing Fashion Editor for GQ magazine: "In Britain we are still very tied up with that idea of masculinity that is almost so fragile that it can be dented by carrying a bag."
sentences.chinese: 据《GQ》杂志特约时尚编辑尼克・卡维尔（Nick Carvell）说：“在英国，我们仍然非常纠结于那种男子气概的观念，这种观念几乎如此脆弱，以至于背个包都能被削弱。”

sentences.english: So, while some British men might think a manbag to be effeminate and not very 'macho', he thinks that many Europeans don't have an issue with toting such a fashionable item.
sentences.chinese: 所以，虽然一些英国男性可能认为男士包娘娘腔（effeminate），不太有“男子气概”（macho），但他认为很多欧洲人对携带（toting）这样一个时尚单品并不在意。

sentences.english: Of course, if I was to exchange my old backpack for a manbag, it would come at a price.
sentences.chinese: 当然，如果我要用旧背包换一个男士包，那可得付出一定的代价（花高价）。

sentences.english: With people like Louis Vuitton, Fendi, Gucci and Dolce and Gabbana designing these bags, they can come with a hefty price tag.
sentences.chinese: 像路易威登（Louis Vuitton）、芬迪（Fendi）、古驰（Gucci）和杜嘉班纳（Dolce and Gabbana）这些品牌所设计出来的包，价格可能会很高昂（hefty）。

sentences.english: I suppose that's the price of fashion!
sentences.chinese: 我想这就是时尚的代价！

sentences.english: And apparently, if I had any spare cash, I could complete my designer outfit by buying a murse – that's a man's purse!
sentences.chinese: 而且显然，如果我有闲钱，我可以买一个murse来搭配我的设计师潮服——也就是男士用的钱包！

sentences.english: I suppose fashions change and we have come a long way from the days when men carried their things in a very masculine briefcase - sturdy, sensible and practical.
sentences.chinese: 我想时尚在变化，男性用非常有男子气概，结实、朴素又实用的公文包来装东西的那个时代已经过去了很久。

sentences.english: Now, it seems, we have to put as much thought into buying a bag as we do into buying our clothes.
sentences.chinese: 现在，似乎我们在买包时要像买衣服一样深思熟虑。

title: The niche food festivals of the UK
titleChinese: 英国多种多样的小众美食节
paragraphs: What do you think of when you hear the word ‘festival’? Is it music? Maybe it’s film. Or could it be food? Food festivals are a common occurrence in the UK and take place in all sorts of places and at all sorts of times: from Taste of London, in Regent’s Park each June to Aldeburgh Food Festival in Suffolk in September. Whatever your taste, there’s a food festival to match – no matter how specialised.

Are you a bit of a carnivore? Then why not try Meatopia. This three-day, London-based festival takes place at the end of August and is a meat lover's paradise. In addition to a range of ethically sourced meat products, from juicy burgers to succulent steaks, attendees can listen to live music, watch butchery demos, and attend informal meat-based workshops.

If you prefer a festival that will help you meet your five a day, then Vegfest is for you. This vegan-friendly event takes place in a range of UK venues several times a year. Here you can enjoy a wide selection of freshly prepared vegan food, learn culinary tips and hear talks on nutrition to help you make the most of your plant-based grub.

If that weren’t niche enough, what about a festival that is dedicated solely to marmalade? Held in Cumbria, this tangy, zesty festival of preserves has been running for 13 years. It includes a competition to find the best homemade marmalade. There are thousands of entries from over 30 different countries across the globe.

If you’d prefer something with a little more kick to it, then you could attend The Ginger and Spice Festival held in Market Drayton. It celebrates its town’s historic connection to Robert Clive, who returned from India with ginger. Because of this, they specialise in baking gingerbread, but also sell a range of artisan spices from mild to hot.

If you have a sweet tooth, then it could be that the National Honey Show, which started in 1921 and is the largest event of its kind, is the place for you to be. This three-day event attracts over 2000 entrants to their traditional competition, and offers lectures and workshops on beekeeping and, of course, that gooey, syrupy golden nectar, honey.

While there’s no accounting for taste, the UK has something to offer most people. From large-scale festivities, to the smaller more amateur gatherings, one thing is certain: people are passionate about their food. And while some of the products on offer might be an acquired taste, when food is given that much attention, it’s unlikely to leave a bad taste in anyone’s mouth.

vocabulary.term: occurrence
vocabulary.entry: occurrence /əˈkʌrəns/ n. 事件；发生的事情
vocabulary.example: Earthquakes are a rare occurrence in this region.
vocabulary.translation: 地震在这个地区是罕见的事件。

vocabulary.term: specialised
vocabulary.entry: specialised /ˈspeʃəlaɪzd/ adj. 专门的；小众的
vocabulary.example: She works in a specialised field of medicine.
vocabulary.translation: 她在医学的一个专门领域工作。

vocabulary.term: carnivore

vocabulary.term: juicy

vocabulary.translation: 这些西红柿真的多汁又美味。

vocabulary.term: succulent
vocabulary.entry: succulent /ˈsʌkjələnt/ adj. 多汁的；鲜嫩的
vocabulary.example: The restaurant serves succulent grilled prawns.
vocabulary.translation: 这家餐厅供应鲜嫩多汁的烤虾。

vocabulary.entry: butchery demos /ˈbʊtʃəri ˈdeməʊz/ n. 屠宰演示（复数）

vocabulary.translation: 美食节上有专业厨师的屠宰演示。

vocabulary.term: vegan-friendly
vocabulary.entry: vegan-friendly /ˈviːɡən ˈfrendli/ adj. 纯素食友好的
vocabulary.example: This café has a great selection of vegan-friendly dishes.
vocabulary.translation: 这家咖啡馆有很多纯素食友好的菜品选择。

vocabulary.term: culinary tips
vocabulary.entry: culinary tips /ˈkʌlɪnəri tɪps/ n. 烹饪技巧（复数）
vocabulary.example: The chef shared some useful culinary tips in the interview.
vocabulary.translation: 这位厨师在采访中分享了一些实用的烹饪技巧。

vocabulary.term: nutrition
vocabulary.entry: nutrition /njuːˈtrɪʃn/ n. 营养
vocabulary.example: Good nutrition is essential for children's growth.
vocabulary.translation: 良好的营养对儿童的成长至关重要。

vocabulary.term: grub
vocabulary.entry: grub /ɡrʌb/ n. 食物（非正式用法）
vocabulary.example: Let's get some grub before the movie starts.
vocabulary.translation: 电影开始前我们找点吃的吧。

vocabulary.term: niche
vocabulary.entry: niche /nɪtʃ/ adj. 小众的；特定领域的
vocabulary.example: The brand caters to a niche market of eco-conscious consumers.
vocabulary.translation: 该品牌面向有环保意识的小众消费者市场。

vocabulary.term: marmalade
vocabulary.entry: marmalade /ˈmɑːməleɪd/ n. 橘子酱
vocabulary.example: She had toast with marmalade for breakfast.
vocabulary.translation: 她早餐吃了涂橘子酱的吐司。

vocabulary.term: tangy
vocabulary.entry: tangy /ˈtændʒi/ adj. 味道浓烈的；酸的
vocabulary.example: The soup has a tangy flavor from the lemon and herbs.
vocabulary.translation: 这汤因加入了柠檬和香草而味道浓烈。

vocabulary.term: zesty
vocabulary.entry: zesty /ˈzesti/ adj. 充满风味的；提神的
